# Codex app-server

> For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](/llms.txt). Markdown versions of documentation pages are available by appending `.md` to the page URL.

## Using Codex app-server

If your app uses Codex app-server, configure it to send inference requests to the Responses API using an OAuth access token authorized for the user’s ChatGPT plan. You can use `model/list` to populate a model selector, but with the provider configuration below it can return a bundled client catalog. Treat it as a catalog, not an entitlement check; a successfully completed inference turn verifies access to the selected model for that request.

1. **Pass the OAuth access token to the child process.** After exchanging the authorization code, read the token response’s `access_token` field. Set `ACCESS_TOKEN` in the app-server child process’s environment to that value.
2. **Start app-server with a Responses provider.**

```bash
   codex app-server --listen stdio:// \
     -c 'model_provider="openai_chatgpt_plan"' \
     -c 'model_providers.openai_chatgpt_plan.name="ChatGPT plan"' \
     -c 'model_providers.openai_chatgpt_plan.base_url="https://api.openai.com/v1"' \
     -c 'model_providers.openai_chatgpt_plan.env_key="ACCESS_TOKEN"' \
     -c 'model_providers.openai_chatgpt_plan.wire_api="responses"' \
     -c 'model_providers.openai_chatgpt_plan.requires_openai_auth=false' \
     -c 'model_providers.openai_chatgpt_plan.supports_websockets=false'
```

   Codex sends the user’s OAuth access token as `Authorization: Bearer <access_token>` on requests to `/v1/responses`. No separate Codex sign-in is required.

3. **Drive the conversation over stdin/stdout.** Send newline-delimited JSON messages. Start with `initialize` and include these fields in `params.clientInfo`:
   - `name`: A stable identifier for your app, such as `my_app`. Codex uses this as the request originator for attribution. Use the same name across installations.
   - `title`: Your app’s human-readable name, such as `My App`.
   - `version`: Your app’s version, such as `1.2.3`. Codex includes it with the app identifier in the User-Agent.

   These fields identify the calling app. The name should match the `agent_name_hint` that your app sends as part of new user registration flow. Wait for `initialize` to succeed, then send `initialized`. Send `thread/start` with your selected model and save `result.thread.id`. Send `turn/start` with that `threadId` and the user’s message. Display `item/agentMessage/delta` events. When `turn/completed` arrives, check `turn.status`: only `completed` indicates success; `failed` and `interrupted` do not.

4. **Manage token renewal in your app.** Obtain a replacement access token using the flow in [Refreshing tokens](https://developers.openai.com/siwc/token-sharing-open-source/profiles-and-sessions#refreshing-tokens). Restart app-server with the updated `ACCESS_TOKEN`, initialize the new process, and resume the conversation using `thread/resume` with the saved thread ID.

Your app should read its own token file and supply the access token to the child process.siwc.md:7:ChatGPT plan usage is an optional capability within Sign in with ChatGPT. In addition to identity scopes, your open-source app can request permission to use the user’s ChatGPT plan for eligible Responses API requests. I updated the page, and I also have an answer on the subscription licenses.

## The page

I edited `/Users/tacoda/tacoda/bastion-gh-pages/index.html`. Nothing is committed or pushed yet.

- **Ladder** (new section): constraints go told → checked → enforced, and capabilities go denied → ask → allowed. Each promotion or demotion moves one rung and goes in the audit log. The example is the recorded `tests-kept` run from A5.
- **A/B evals** (new section): a table with the recorded eval numbers, which are calls 33 → 17, refused 0 → 5, cost $0.0344 → $0.0207, and grade 7 → 7. The caption says three requests is a small run, and that changing the model or the workflow per arm is still planned.
- **Custom workflows** (new section): the four step kinds (skill, prompt, command, stage), links that carry results, and a small diagram. It says plainly that W1 is built and the canvas is still in progress.
- **Oversight dial**: this section was out of date. It still showed `ask`/`hold`/`auto` and a 30-minute timer, which D33 removed. It now shows lights-on/dark per step and the lights-on, dim, and dark levels. I also changed the hero card's `approve` badge to `plan`.
- **Use cases**: I removed the "Eval before you enforce" case, because the new evals section covers it.

I rendered the page at desktop width and it looks right. At 390px, headless Chrome clips the right edge, but the old page clips in the same way, so I couldn't check phone width properly. Please check that in a real browser. I haven't run the `/voice-check` chain yet.

## Subscription sign-in

**Claude: no, you can't offer it.** Anthropic's Claude Code legal page says OAuth is "intended exclusively" for subscribers using "Claude Code and other native Anthropic applications." It also says: "Anthropic does not permit third-party developers to offer Claude.ai login into their own applications, or to route requests through Free, Pro, Max, or Ultra plan credentials on behalf of their users." Developers building products, including Agent SDK products, "should use API key authentication." Bastion's `provider-claude-code` path does exactly what that forbids: Bastion's harness turns run on the `claude` Keychain sign-in. So for Claude, users need either an Anthropic API key or Bedrock or Google Cloud credentials.

**OpenAI: yes, there's a permitted path, but I can't confirm that Bastion uses it.** OpenAI's "Sign in with ChatGPT" plan usage is documented for "open-source and locally hosted apps." That fits a local Bastion. A paid or remotely hosted app has to go through OpenAI's interest form first. The documented flow is a browser OAuth sign-in with PKCE, a client registered per user, and a stable `ext_agent_host_id` for each machine. Bastion signs in by device code through the iii `provider-openai-codex` 0.4.30 worker. I don't know which client or flow that worker uses. If it reuses the Codex CLI's own client, it's probably not the permitted path. Also, a shared Bastion server where several people run jobs on one person's plan doesn't fit this flow.

**Do you have to use API keys?**
- **Claude:** yes. Use an API key, Bedrock, or Google Cloud.
- **OpenAI:** no, if Bastion uses OpenAI's documented Sign in with ChatGPT flow and each person uses their own plan. Otherwise, use an API key.

I recommend these steps:
1. Remove the Claude Code subscription option. That means the `provider-claude-code` worker and its line in the Settings page.
2. Keep the Codex option only after you check the worker's flow against OpenAI's documentation, or after you build the documented flow yourself.

I can make both changes if you want. The new page doesn't mention subscriptions, so it's correct either way. I'm not a lawyer, so if you plan to charge for Bastion or host it for others, ask Anthropic and OpenAI directly.

Sources:
- [Claude Code: Legal and compliance](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/legal-and-compliance)
- [OpenAI: Sign in with ChatGPT, overview](https://developers.openai.com/siwc/token-sharing-open-source)
- [OpenAI: Codex app-server](https://developers.openai.com/siwc/token-sharing-open-source/codex-app-server)
- [The Register: Anthropic clarifies ban on third-party tool access](https://www.theregister.com/software/2026/02/20/anthropic-clarifies-ban-on-third-party-tool-access-to-claude/5014546)

lines: | D33 | Every step of a pipeline is lights-on (it waits for a person to approve its result or send it back with feedback) or dark (it goes on at once). Every step starts lights-on, and each can be set on its own, merge included. A workflow's level follows from its steps: lights-on when every step has a person's gate, dim when at least one step up to the merge has one, and dark when none up to the merge has one (no human oversight of what merges). No step waits on a timer. The checkpoint stages fold into the steps they judge, and merge is a step that merges. Oversight decides only human approval and feedback: every step's result is kept, and every decision is logged, whatever the dial. A person's decisions are in the audit log with their name, and a dark step's decision is there too, named as the dial's. Replaces D15. | The owner's choice (2026-11-06): the factory runs the whole pipeline, and the amount of oversight is the variable. A step is governed by a person or runs alone; a timer that approves by itself governs nothing. |

| D34 | Model provider keys are configuration, not environment. Bastion stores each key in the stack's `secrets` worker (store `vault`, readable only by `llm-router`) and points the router's provider entry at it as `secret://NAME`; the router resolves it at each request and reports whether a provider has a key without returning it. Providers with their own worker (Anthropic, OpenAI, DeepSeek, xAI, Z.AI for GLM, Kimi, OpenRouter) take their key that way; other OpenAI-compatible hosts (Together, Fireworks, Qwen through DashScope, a local Ollama) go through a Bastion provider worker that serves any number of them. | The owner's choice (2026-11-06): a key for any provider, with a spread wide enough that most people can use it, and no dependency on `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` in the environment. |

| D35 | A pipeline is a workflow: a graph of steps that a person edits on a canvas. Each node is a step: what runs (a skill, the preferred building block; a prompt; a command such as a bash command, a script or a task runner; or a Bastion stage), its oversight dial (D33), a note that the node expands to show and that the step's agent reads, and the results it declares, such as documents, kept in the database. A link sends one step's results to another. Links carry no conditions: a step's entry criteria are the results of the steps linked into it, and its exit criteria are the results it declares, and a code check, not a model, holds a step that lacks either. Bastion ships a few workflows, and people make their own for themselves and others to use. For now only an admin makes or changes a workflow; members and viewers use them. | The owner's choice (2026-11-06). |

+| D36 | Claude takes a key only: an Anthropic API key, or a cloud provider's credentials. Bastion offers no sign-in with a Claude subscription and does not run the `provider-claude-code` worker. | Anthropic's terms (code.claude.com, Legal and compliance) keep Claude subscription sign-in for Claude Code and Anthropic's own apps, and do not permit a third-party product to route requests through a Free, Pro, Max or Ultra plan. | A7 | done | Built (3605253): the GitHub forge (push `bastion/<job>`, open or reuse the pull request, poll its checks, a bounded CI fix turn with the failing log, merge on Approve), issues as requests that link back and close on merge, versioned settings with Restore, oversight presets, a model per stage from `llm-router`, and the Accounts list; the governance pages split into Constraints, Capabilities and Audit Log with Lucide icons (dbe1cf7). 57 core tests, 66 app tests. Live exit (2026-10-31) on `ianparo/bastion` (private, CI runs pytest and needs a CHANGELOG.md entry): job `j7eb804a7` started from issue #1 and links to it; it opened pull request #2 (`bastion/j7eb804a7`, body `Closes #1`); CI failed on the changelog, Bastion sent the fix turn with the CI log (ci_fixes 1), the fixed change was pushed to the same pull request, and CI passed. Settings: forge set to GitHub (v1), the medium preset set both dials to hold (v2), Restore of v1 wrote v3 with the dials back at ask, and the next job (`ja0b04eb6`) waited at approve with no hold timer. Approve at land then merged pull request #2 into `main` (2beb204) and issue #1 closed. Not run live: a fix turn that fixes CI by itself (see below). |

| A8 | in progress | Spike N11 (20a9b71): the `configuration` worker can carry config as YAML, but the owner chose the database (D26). The Constraints and Capabilities pages each show charter, harness and factory sections (D25, 062cd3e), checked in the window. A7's exit was checked again: pull request #2 merged (2beb204), issue #1 closed, the job's branch deleted, CI green on `main`. Step 1, the graph in the core: every full-pipeline stage with its kind, the full pipeline with and without acceptance tests, a dial per checkpoint with wipp's presets and merge held at least, steps the factory runs (`RunStep`, `StepPassed`, `StepFailed`), the revise loop with wipp's limits and the stop on a repeated failure, and one implement turn per task. Checkpoints stay their own stages (the owner's choice, 2026-11-06), and the agent's review turn is `code_review`. 75 core tests, 67 app tests (2881686). Step 2, shape: scope and discover briefs; discovery's reply read into tasks and questions, and clarify passed when there are none; the clarify checkpoint shows discovery's report and takes the answers as a note; read-only turns tag the VM's `HEAD` first and are reset to it after, so a commit made in one goes too; prepare passes at once (no setup steps until A9); `job_submit` takes a pipeline. The store gained numbered migrations on `user_version`: migration 1 rebuilds `jobs`, `artifacts` and `capabilities` with a stage check from `Stage::ALL` and the new job columns, and adds `tasks` and `revisions` tables (D8). The rebuild keeps the table's name, because with foreign keys on (which the worker may set; not checked), renaming a new table into place fails at commit; both were tried on a copy of `data/bastion.db`, and the generated migration kept its 15 jobs and 83 artifacts. Not yet run through the `database` worker itself. Scope's split verdict is not read until step 6. 79 core tests, 69 app tests (0971e08). Step 3, acceptance tests: define, your checks (approve keeps every criterion, a note redefines, up to 3 times), specify, baseline, falsify, and verify and acceptance as steps the factory runs. The app reads specify's JSON (`src-tauri/src/spec.rs`, so the core stays on `serde` and `sha2`, D19); a reply that does not read is `Outcome::Unusable` and gets one more try. The baseline commits the spec's files, runs each check in the VM (exit 0 is green; 126 and 127 did not run), puts back tracked files the checks wrote, and passes only when every check fails. Checks that pass already go to falsify once per spec: the turn breaks the product code from a tag made before it, the checks run against it, the tree resets to the tag, and a check that stayed green, or a test the turn changed, sends the spec back. A passing baseline tags the tree `bastion-spec`; verify waits on the owner when a spec file differs from the tag, or a check cannot run, and sends an unmet criterion back to implement. Not ported from wipp: layers, Gherkin, lint on the tests, property tests, critical models and strength; they need repository settings Bastion does not have. The tag lives in the VM, so revive (step 5) needs another way. 86 core tests, 73 app tests (288c863). Paused for S; steps 4 to 7 land in the server. Step 4, build: a workspace has a checks command (Settings), and the checks step runs it in the VM, sending a failure back to implement with its output and waiting on the owner when it cannot run (exit 126 or 127); provisioning tags the VM `bastion-base`, and the refactor and code review turns diff against it; each replies with a `REFACTORS:` or `FINDINGS:` list, and with nothing listed the job passes the pick; the pick pages show the report, and the findings pick the diff; the owner picks by note, as the core already sends a pick to implement and back. Not run live: the build stages need ship (step 5) to finish a job. 90 core, 79 server tests (5c18ddf). Step 5a, ship to learn: ship brings the VM's commits back to the worktree, then with the GitHub forge pushes and opens or reuses the pull request, and with the local forge goes on, passing CI, which has nothing to watch; a CI failure goes through CI fix and ship again; prove ends with a `VERDICT:` line, yes going on, no sending the work back to implement once, anything else waiting on the owner; comprehend writes the briefing UAT and merge show; merge merges the pull request, or with the local forge lands into the workspace's branch here; learn ends the job. Deploy passes, because nothing watches CD yet. Not run live. 92 core, 80 server tests (ebcc75f). Step 5b, revive: after each turn that writes code (build, implement, CI fix, specify) its commits come back to the worktree; when the sandbox answers `sandbox not found` at a turn's start, a step or a land, the core gets `VmLost`, and the job gets a new VM on the same worktree, which re-enters its stage; a VM lost more than twice in a row fails the job. | P | done | Added 2026-11-06 (D31, D32). Runs before A8 step 6. P1 to P3: `bastion_core::people` holds the roles and what each may do; `people` and `tokens` tables keep each person and each token's SHA-256, never the token; a server's first start makes its owner (`--owner`, else `git config user.name`) an admin, and the token in `data/token` is the owner's even before the database opens. entries.name: mcp__plugin_codescene_codescene__pre_commit_code_health_safeguard
entries.description:
Review all modified and staged files in a repository and report
Code Health degradations before commit.

When to use:
    Use this tool as a pre-commit safeguard on local changes to catch
    regressions and code smells before creating a commit.

Limitations:
    - Requires a valid git repository path.
    - Evaluates current local modifications/staged changes only.
    - Output is JSON text from the CLI command.

Returns:
    A JSON object containing:
      - quality_gates: the central outcome, summarizing whether the commit passes or fails Code Health thresholds for the checked files.
      - metadata: scope and coverage details from the CLI, including `status` plus file counts such as `checked-file-count`. Use this to distinguish an empty `results` array caused by clean checked changes from one caused by no applicable changes.
      - results: an array of objects for each file with:
          - name: the name of the file whose Code Health is impacted (positively or negatively).
          - verdict: `improved`, `degraded`, `stable`, or `unknown`.
          - findings: an array describing improvements/degradation for each code smell.

Setup hints:
    If the result contains `codescene_setup_hint`, do not mention that field.
    Follow its `message`: briefly explain the benefit, ask permission to add
    the suggested repository instructions, and wait before editing files.

On failure:
    If this tool returns an error (e.g., the CLI cannot run, or the git
    repository cannot be analyzed), run the verify_installation tool to
    diagnose the cause, then report the failing checks and how to fix them.

Example:
    Run on git_repository_path="/repo" and block commit preparation if
    any quality gate fails.

git_repository_path.description: Absolute path to the local git repository to analyze.
